inlines.text: A survey of 200 people was carried out to determine hair and eye colour. The results are shown in the table below.
What is the probability that a person chosen at random from this group has:

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}P(\text{blue eyes})&=\frac{25+9+6+18}{200}\\P(\text{blue eyes})&=\frac{58}{200}\\P(\text{blue eyes})&=\frac{29}{100}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}P(\text{red hair})&=\frac{6+18+22}{200}\\P(\text{red hair})&=\frac{46}{200}\\P(\text{red hair})&=\frac{23}{100}\end{align*}$$

Fair hair: $25+16+15=56$. Brown hair: $9+16+17=42$. These hair categories are mutually exclusive.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{fair or brown hair})&=\frac{56+42}{200}\\P(\text{fair or brown hair})&=\frac{49}{100}\end{align*}$$

Blue eyes: $25+9+6+18=58$. Brown eyes: $16+16+18+22=72$. These eye categories are mutually exclusive.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{blue or brown eyes})&=\frac{58+72}{200}\\P(\text{blue or brown eyes})&=\frac{13}{20}\end{align*}$$

The red-hair, green-eyes cell contains 22 people.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{red hair and green eyes})&=\frac{22}{200}\\P(\text{red hair and green eyes})&=\frac{11}{100}\end{align*}$$

Green eyes: $15+17+22+16=70$.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{not green eyes})&=1-P(\text{green eyes})\\P(\text{not green eyes})&=1-\frac{70}{200}\\P(\text{not green eyes})&=\frac{13}{20}\end{align*}$$

Red hair: $6+18+22=46$.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{not red hair})&=1-P(\text{red hair})\\P(\text{not red hair})&=1-\frac{46}{200}\\P(\text{not red hair})&=\frac{77}{100}\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
The only people excluded have both blue eyes and fair hair: 25 people. Everyone else satisfies at least one of the two conditions.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{not blue eyes or not fair hair})&=1-P(\text{blue eyes and fair hair})\\P(\text{not blue eyes or not fair hair})&=1-\frac{25}{200}\\P(\text{not blue eyes or not fair hair})&=\frac{7}{8}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}n(S\cap T^c)&=19-5\\n(S\cap T^c)&=14\\P(S\cap T^c)&=\frac{14}{40}=\frac{7}{20}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Two dice are rolled and the results are noted. What is the probability that:

children.label: a
children.prompt: the sum of the numbers is odd?

answer.worked:
There are $6\times6=36$ equally likely ordered outcomes. An odd sum requires one odd number and one even number. There are $3\times3=9$ outcomes in each order, giving $18$ favourable outcomes.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{odd sum})&=\frac{18}{36}\\P(\text{odd sum})&=\frac12\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: the product of the numbers is even?

answer.worked:
The product is even when at least one result is even. In the $6\times6$ outcome array, the three even-numbered rows contain $18$ outcomes. The three odd-numbered rows each contain another $3$ outcomes with an even second result. Thus there are $18+9=27$ favourable outcomes.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{even product})&=\frac{27}{36}\\P(\text{even product})&=\frac34\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: the difference of the two numbers is 2?

answer.worked:
Taking the larger number minus the smaller, the favourable ordered outcomes are $(1,3)$, $(2,4)$, $(3,5)$, $(4,6)$, $(3,1)$, $(4,2)$, $(5,3)$ and $(6,4)$.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{difference is }2)&=\frac{8}{36}\\P(\text{difference is }2)&=\frac29\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: the sum of the numbers is greater than 9?

answer.worked:
The favourable ordered outcomes are $(4,6)$, $(5,5)$ and $(6,4)$ for a sum of $10$; $(5,6)$ and $(6,5)$ for a sum of $11$; and $(6,6)$ for a sum of $12$.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{sum greater than }9)&=\frac{6}{36}\\P(\text{sum greater than }9)&=\frac16\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: one of the numbers is 3 and the sum of the numbers is less than 6?

answer.worked:
If one result is $3$, the other must be $1$ or $2$ for the sum to be less than $6$. The favourable ordered outcomes are $(3,1)$, $(3,2)$, $(1,3)$ and $(2,3)$.

Only AH is favourable among the 10 equally likely outcomes.

answer.worked:
The tree gives eight equally likely outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH and TTT. Only TTT has no head, so seven outcomes contain at least one head.

$$P(\text{at least one head})=\frac{7}{8}.$$

children.prompt: How many outcomes are there? (Hint: Try to picture what the tree diagram would look like without actually drawing it.)

answer.worked:
Each toss doubles the number of paths in the tree.

$$\text{Number of outcomes}=2\times2\times2\times2=16.$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: What is the probability that at least one head is obtained?

answer.worked:
Of the 16 equally likely outcomes, only TTTT has no head. Therefore 15 outcomes contain at least one head.

$$P(\text{at least one head})=\frac{16-1}{16}=\frac{15}{16}.$$

There are two possible results at each of the $n$ stages, so the number of terminal paths doubles at each stage.

$$\text{Number of outcomes}=2^n.$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: What is the probability that at least one head is obtained?

answer.short:
$\frac{2^n-1}{2^n}$

Exclude the single outcome consisting entirely of tails.
answer.worked:
There are $2^n$ equally likely outcomes. Exactly one has no heads: tails on every toss. Thus $2^n-1$ outcomes contain at least one head.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{at least one head})&=\frac{2^n-1}{2^n}\\P(\text{at least one head})&=1-\frac{1}{2^n}.\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: For each event state the following:
What is the probability that no sixes are obtained?
What is the probability that at least one six is obtained?

answer.worked: Each die has six possible results, so the number of ordered outcomes is $6\times6\times6=216$.

Each die has five results other than six, giving $5^3=125$ favourable outcomes.

$$P(\text{no sixes})=\frac{5^3}{6^3}=\frac{125}{216}.$$

The complement of obtaining at least one six is obtaining no sixes.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{at least one six})&=1-\frac{125}{216}\\P(\text{at least one six})&=\frac{91}{216}.\end{align*}$$
Each die has six possible results, so the number of ordered outcomes is $6^4=1296$.

Each die has five results other than six, giving $5^4=625$ favourable outcomes.

$$P(\text{no sixes})=\frac{5^4}{6^4}=\frac{625}{1296}.$$

The complement of obtaining at least one six is obtaining no sixes.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{at least one six})&=1-\frac{625}{1296}\\P(\text{at least one six})&=\frac{671}{1296}.\end{align*}$$
There are six choices at each of $n$ stages, so the number of ordered outcomes is $6^n$.

answer.short:
$\left(\frac56\right)^n$

Count five non-six choices for each die out of six possible choices.
answer.worked:
There are $5^n$ outcomes containing no sixes and $6^n$ equally likely outcomes in total.

$$P(\text{no sixes})=\frac{5^n}{6^n}=\left(\frac56\right)^n.$$

answer.short:
$1-\left(\frac56\right)^n$

Subtract the probability of no sixes from 1.
answer.worked:
The events ‘no sixes’ and ‘at least one six’ are complementary.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{at least one six})&=1-P(\text{no sixes})\\P(\text{at least one six})&=1-\left(\frac56\right)^n.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: In a certain town there are 100000 cars, each having a licence plate number from 1 to 100000. What is the probability that the first car you see on a given day does not have a 6 or 7 in its number plate?

answer.short:
$\dfrac{1024}{3125}$

Count five-position strings allowing leading zeros, then replace 00000 with 100000; both avoid 6 and 7.
answer.worked:
Write the numbers from 0 to 99999 using five digit positions, allowing leading zeros. Each position has eight permitted digits: $0,1,2,3,4,5,8,9$.

$$\begin{align*}N(\text{permitted strings})&=8\times8\times8\times8\times8\\N(\text{permitted strings})&=32768\end{align*}$$

The stated range excludes 00000 and includes 100000. Both avoid 6 and 7, so the number of favourable plates is unchanged.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{no 6 or 7})&=\frac{32768-1+1}{100000}\\P(\text{no 6 or 7})&=\frac{32768}{100000}\\P(\text{no 6 or 7})&=\frac{1024}{3125}\end{align*}$$

Probability measures the likelihood of an event occurring on a scale from 0 to 1, inclusive.
In this section we look at methods for determining probabilities. We recall some ideas from ICE-EM Mathematics Year 8.

entries.description:
An event is a collection of outcomes. It is a subset of the sample space.
Suppose that for the experiment above we are interested in getting a prime number. In this case ‘the number is prime’ is the event that interests us. Some of the outcomes will give rise to this event. For instance, if the outcome of the experiment is 2, the event ‘the number is prime’ takes place. We say that the outcome 2 is favourable to the event ‘the number is prime’. If the outcome is 4, the event ‘the number is prime’ does not occur. The outcome 4 is not favourable to the event.
Of the 12 outcomes, these are the ones that are favourable to the event ‘the number is prime’:
{2, 3, 5, 7, 11}
In many situations, ‘success’ means ‘favourable to the event’ and ‘failure’ means ‘not favourable to the event’.

entries.description:
Probability of an event
The probability of the event A is written P(A).
Since the probability of an event is a number between 0 and 1 inclusive, we can assert:
0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1 for all events A
For an experiment in which all of the outcomes are equally likely:
Probability of an event = (number of outcomes favourable to that event)/(total number of outcomes)
For the event B described above, P(B) = 5/12.
In general, the probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of the outcomes that are favourable to that event.

entries.description:
The words ‘random’ and ‘randomly’
In probability, we frequently hear these words, as in the following situation.
A classroom contains 23 students. A teacher comes into the room and chooses a student at random to answer a question about history.
What does this mean? It means that the teacher chooses the student as if the teacher knows nothing at all about the students. Another way of interpreting this is to imagine that the teacher had her eyes closed and had no idea who was in the class when she choose a student. Each student is equally likely to be chosen. The probability of a particular student being chosen is 1/23.

entries.description:
The complement of an event
In some problems the outcomes in the event A can be difficult to count, whereas the event ‘not A’ may be easier to deal with.
The event ‘not A’ consists of every possible outcome in the sample space ξ that is not in A. The set ‘not A’ is called the complement of A and is denoted by A^c.
Every outcome of a sample space is contained in exactly one of A or A^c.
Therefore P(A) + P(A^c) = 1 and P(A^c) = 1 − P(A).
This can be illustrated with a Venn diagram, as shown.

entries.description:
Estimates of probability

If we find a coin on the street that is badly worn and bent by the weather and passing traffic, it would not be reasonable to assume that a Head and Tail are equally likely to occur when we toss the coin. So we would have no idea of what the probability of a Head would be.

One way of attempting to get around the difficulty is to toss the coin a large number of times and record how many Heads occur. If we tossed the coin 100 times, we might get these results:
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone teaching introducing experimental estimates; no assigned practice task.

entries.description:
Heads: 40    Tails: 60

Then we could divide to get \(\frac{40}{100}=\frac25\) as an estimate of the probability of getting a Head.

This is called relative frequency.

The relative frequency of getting a Tail is therefore \(\frac35\).

We are going to use relative frequency as an estimate of the probability for future experiments. So in this case, our estimate for the probability of getting a Head is \(\frac25\).
